summary: A Washington Post analysis by Shannon Osaka, published September 30, 2023, uses a thought experiment to explore what would happen if the world suddenly stopped extracting fossil fuels. It concludes that an abrupt halt would be catastrophic, with blackouts and food shortages within weeks, so most activists instead call for preventing new oil, gas and coal extraction. The article also notes that phasing out fossil fuels must be balanced against the buildout of renewables, and that the Biden administration's plans and worker transition concerns complicate the timing.
one_line: A Washington Post analysis of what a sudden or planned end to fossil fuel extraction would mean for grids, food supply and workers.
key_facts: The world produces roughly 36.5 billion barrels of oil in a given year and over 8 billion metric tons of coal.
The United States alone extracts and processes over 100 billion cubic feet of natural gas per year.
Samantha Gross, director of the energy security and climate initiative at the Brookings Institution, said of a sudden halt: "Oh, dear God."
The United States' strategic petroleum reserve held around 347 million barrels of oil, enough to last the country just 17 days at current use levels.
The strategic petroleum reserve would last the world just 3½ days.
Kelly Trout, research co-director at Oil Change International, said "The expectation isn't that extraction will stop everywhere in the world."
The International Energy Agency says there is no need for the world to open new coal mines or develop oil and gas projects with long lead times.
Olivier Bois von Kursk of the International Institute for Sustainable Development notes oil and gas fields lose about 4 percent of production each year as reservoir pressure decreases.
The IEA predicts the world will have to triple renewable energy capacity in just seven years to cut fossil fuel demand by 20 percent.
According to Oil Change International, the United States is responsible for around one-third of planned fossil fuel expansion between now and 2050.
On a Friday, the Biden administration unveiled a plan to allow more offshore oil and gas leasing in the Gulf of Mexico over the next five years.
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol worries about workers in coal, oil and gas being left unemployed, warning that a poorly planned transition could cause a backlash with political implications.
Mattea Mrkusic, energy transition policy lead at Evergreen Action, said: "Any new leasing will make the world more dangerous and less prosperous."

Protesters at New York's Climate Week urged world leaders to "end fossil fuels now" and sent a letter to President Biden asking him to commit to phasing out fossil fuel extraction in the United States.
UN Secretary General António Guterres hosted a climate summit where only nations committed to "no new coal, oil and gas" were invited.
